text: Mina puts three pictures on the table. One shows her aunt. One shows her brother. One shows her friend. “These people care for me,” she says. “We read books together. We cook soup together. We water plants together.” Her friend points at the soup picture. “Who holds the spoon?” he asks. “I do,” says Mina. “My aunt holds the bowl.” Mina leaves space for another picture. She wants to add more words later.

words.meaning: things drawn or shown
help someone feel safe and well
with another person
a tool for eating or stirring
an empty place

questions.q: Who is in the first picture?
What do they cook?
What does Mina hold?

talk: What do you enjoy doing with other people?
How can a person show they care?
title: People Around Me

text: In the morning, Jo opens the curtains. His uncle makes breakfast. “Please pass the cups,” says his uncle. Jo puts two cups on the table. Then they eat and talk. In the evening, their jobs change. Jo washes the cups. His uncle dries them with a towel. “What comes next?” asks Jo. “Our book,” says his uncle. They sit on the sofa and read. Some days are busy, but they keep this quiet time.

words.meaning: cloth that covers a window
the first meal of the day
takes water off something
cloth for drying
with little noise

questions.q: Who opens the curtains?
What does Jo wash?
Where do they read?

talk: What do you do at the start of a day?
Which quiet activity would you share, and why?
title: Home Routines

text: It is a free day. Ali wants to play outside. His cousin wants to draw. Their grandmother wants to rest. “We need a plan,” says Ali. His cousin brings some paper to the garden. Ali finds a ball. Their grandmother sits under a tree. First, the cousins draw the tree together. Next, they play with the ball. Later, they show their grandmother the picture. “We all have a part,” she says. Everyone smiles.

words.meaning: a child of your aunt or uncle
stop working and relax
ideas for what to do
a place where plants grow
something one person does

questions.q: Who wants to draw?
Where does their grandmother sit?
What do the cousins draw?

talk: How would you plan a day for different people?
What activity could everyone enjoy together?
title: Our Shared Day

text: Mina finds her three pictures again. At first, she only named the people. Now she adds what each person does. “My aunt reads slowly with me,” she says. “My brother chops carrots while I stir soup.” She points at the last picture. “My friend carries water, and I water the plants.” Her friend listens. “We help each other in different ways,” he says. Mina writes that sentence under the pictures. Her little guide is ready.

words.meaning: said what someone is called
not quickly
cuts into small pieces
move a spoon through food
something that helps people understand

questions.q: How does Mina's aunt read?
What does her brother chop?
What does her friend carry?

talk: What can you explain more clearly about a shared activity?
How could you help someone join that activity?
title: What We Can Say Now

text: Nia opens the animal card she made in the first lesson. It says, “A penguin is a bird.” She wants her guide to say more. She adds three clear facts. “Penguins live in groups. They eat fish. They swim using their flippers.” Her partner asks, “Do all penguins live on ice?” Nia checks her notes. “No. Some live in warmer places,” she replies. She draws a penguin on a rocky beach, not beside an ice house. Her guide now shows a home, food and movement. She leaves a question at the bottom for visitors. “What would you like to find out next?”

words.meaning: something that explains a place or subject
sets of people or animals together
flat body parts used for swimming
with more heat
covered with rocks

questions.q: Which animal does Nia describe?
What do penguins eat?
What do penguins use to swim?

talk: Which three facts would you include in an animal guide?
How can a picture help someone understand an animal's home?
title: My Animal Guide

text: A small food club is making a picture menu. Sami draws a bowl of rice with beans and carrots. “This is my favourite meal,” he says. “It is warm. The carrots are sweet. The rice is soft.” His partner draws bread with tomato soup. They ask each other about their choices. Sami likes beans because they make his meal filling. His partner likes soup because she can dip bread into it. They each write three describing words beside their pictures. The menu has room for more meals. Nobody needs to choose the same favourite. The club wants to hear different ideas.

words.meaning: a list of food choices
with a taste like sugar
easy to press or bite
making you feel you have eaten enough
put something briefly into a liquid

questions.q: What does Sami draw?
How do the carrots taste?
What does his partner dip into soup?

talk: How would you describe a meal you enjoy?
What makes different meals enjoyable for different people?
title: My Favourite Meal

text: The food club puts its old picture menu on the table. Sami reads the words beside his rice bowl. Last time, his description used just three short words. Now he tries clearer words. “The rice is soft. The carrots are sweet and crunchy. The beans have a smooth skin.” His partner asks which part she should taste first. “Try a carrot,” says Sami. “Then try it with a little rice.” She describes her soup too. It is warm, thick and full of small tomato pieces. They add their new words to the menu. A visitor can now imagine how both meals taste.

words.meaning: making a noise when you bite
without bumps
not flowing as easily as water
small parts of something
make a picture in your mind

questions.q: Which food is crunchy?
What should Sami's partner try first?
Which food is warm and thick?

talk: Which describing words help you imagine a meal?
How could you improve the description of your first meal?
title: Our Food Table

text: Ravi stands by the classroom window with a blank weather card. He needs three sentences about today. “The sky is grey,” he says. “The air feels cool. Light rain is falling.” His partner listens and looks outside too. She notices small drops on the glass. A tree moves gently in the wind. Ravi draws a cloud, a coat and a raindrop. The pictures help him remember his report. He writes his three sentences under them. He will keep this card until the course ends. Another day may look very different. For now, his report tells the class what he can see and feel.

words.meaning: a colour between black and white
a little cold
in a soft, calm way
one small drop of rain
a short account of what you notice

questions.q: What colour is the sky?
How does the air feel?
What helps Ravi remember?

talk: What three sentences would describe the weather around you?
What signs could help you decide what to wear outside?
title: The Weather Today

text: Ravi brings back his first weather card. It shows grey clouds and light rain. Today, the sky looks different. “Thin clouds are moving past the Sun,” he reports. “The air feels warmer than before. A steady wind is moving the leaves.” His partner asks whether they need coats for their walk. Ravi looks at the clouds again. “I will bring a light coat,” he says. “The wind may feel cool in the shade.” He compares his new report with the old one. Both have three main sentences, but the new report gives more detail. The class can use it to plan their afternoon.

words.meaning: not thick
continuing without much change
a place away from direct sunlight
looks at things to find differences
a small piece of information

questions.q: What is moving past the Sun?
What will Ravi bring?
How many main sentences does each report have?

talk: How does today's weather compare with your first report?
Which extra detail would make a weather report more useful?
title: Our Weather Report

text: Lila looks out of her window before bed. The Moon is above the roofs. Several stars shine nearby. “Can I make a space notebook?” she asks. Her brother brings paper. Lila writes three things she can say now. The Moon looks bright. Its shape seems to change across different nights. Stars look like tiny points from here. Her brother asks whether the Moon makes its own light. They find the answer in their space book. It reflects light from the Sun. Lila adds that fact beside her drawing. She leaves another page for a Moon journey she will imagine later.

words.meaning: the tops of buildings
give or show light
the form of something
sends light back from a surface
travel from one place to another

questions.q: Where does Lila look from?
What does Lila want to make?
Where does the Moon's light come from?

talk: What three things would you say about the night sky?
What would you like to find out about the Moon?
title: Look Up Tonight

text: Lila turns to the empty page in her space notebook. She draws an imagined Moon journey. Her first note only described the Moon from Earth. Now her guide follows an astronaut onto its rocky surface. “This round hole is a crater,” she explains. “Our astronaut needs a spacesuit. There is no air to breathe here.” She draws Earth above the astronaut's head. Her brother asks what happens next. “The astronaut collects a small rock,” Lila says. “Then the rocket takes the astronaut home.” She checks three parts of her guide: the place, the equipment and the return. Her space words now tell a whole journey.

words.meaning: the outside or top of something
a round hole in the ground
special clothing for a person in space
things needed for a job
going back to where you started

questions.q: What is the round hole called?
What does the astronaut need?
What does the astronaut collect?

talk: How would you describe your imagined Moon journey?
Which piece of equipment would you explain to a visitor, and why?
title: Our Space Guide

text: Omar finds a dinosaur model in a box. It has a long neck, a small head and four strong legs. He makes a card with three sentences. “This dinosaur is tall. It has a long tail. It walks on four legs.” His partner picks a different model. That one stands on two legs. They put the models beside each other and compare them. Neither model is a real animal, but each helps them notice body parts. Omar leaves the back of his card blank. Later, he wants to add clues from rocks. They can show more than a model.

words.meaning: a small copy of something
the part between head and body
a long part behind an animal
look for similarities and differences
things that help you find an answer

questions.q: What kind of neck does Omar's model have?
How many legs does it walk on?
Which part of the card stays blank?

talk: What three sentences could describe your dinosaur model?
How are a model and a real dinosaur different?
title: Meet a Dinosaur

text: A class visits a small display of old rocks. One rock holds a leaf shape. Another shows three footprints. “Where is the dinosaur?” asks Ada. The guide points at the footprints. “A fossil can be a mark,” she says. “It does not need to be a whole bone.” Ada studies the spaces between the prints. They show where an animal stepped long ago. She cannot learn its colour from these marks. Her friend draws the prints in a notebook. Together, they make two lists: things the rock shows and questions it cannot answer. Their best clue is small, but it tells a real part of a story.

words.meaning: things arranged for people to look at
marks left by feet
an old body part or mark in rock
a sign left on a surface
put a foot down while moving

questions.q: What shape does the first rock hold?
What does the guide point at?
What can Ada not learn from the marks?

talk: What could a footprint tell you about an animal?
How would you explain the difference between a clue and a guess?
title: Clues in the Ground

text: Omar brings his dinosaur card to the class museum. He still uses his three body sentences. Now he adds a separate label for evidence. “These bones show long legs,” he says. “These footprints show steps in the ground.” A visitor asks whether the dinosaur was green. Omar does not invent an answer. “This model is green,” he replies. “Our clues do not show its colour.” He points to a sketch of a feather fossil. Some dinosaurs had feathers, but not every dinosaur was the same. His museum talk now describes an animal and explains what supports his ideas. The blank back of his first card is full.

words.meaning: a short note identifying or explaining something
information that supports an idea
make up something new
a simple drawing
helps show that something may be true

questions.q: Where does Omar take his card?
What do the bones show?
What is the model's colour?

talk: How would you add evidence to your first dinosaur description?
What should a museum guide say when the answer is unknown?
title: My Dinosaur Museum

text: Tess meets a new student at the school gate. “This is our school,” she says. “We read in the classroom. We play in the yard. We eat in the lunch room.” The new student has a small map. Tess points to each place on it. Their teacher waves from the door. “Come and meet the class,” he says. Tess writes her three school sentences on the map. Later, she wants to make a better guide.

words.meaning: a door in a fence
an open space beside a building
a picture showing where places are
moves a hand to say hello
information that helps someone

questions.q: Who does Tess meet?
Where do students play?
Who waves from the door?

talk: What three things would you say about a school day?
Which place would you show a new student first, and why?
title: My School Day

text: Nico wants the blue pencil. His partner is using it. “Can I use it next?” he asks. “Yes, after this line,” she says. Nico waits. Then she passes the pencil to him. Later, she cannot find her ruler. “Can you help me?” she asks. Nico looks under the paper. The ruler is there. “Here it is,” he says. They finish their picture together. Asking and waiting help both students work. Neither person needs to shout.

words.meaning: someone working with you
a long thin mark
stays until something can happen
a tool for measuring straight lines
speak very loudly

questions.q: Which pencil does Nico want?
What is his partner missing?
Where is the ruler?

talk: How could you ask politely for something you need?
What helps partners take turns fairly?
title: Ask and Answer

text: Tess opens her school map again. She adds more help for visitors. “We read in the classroom after morning talk,” she writes. “We take turns with the books. We eat in the lunch room at midday.” She marks the quiet reading corner with a star. A new student asks where to put a bag. Tess shows the hooks beside the door. Her guide tells people where things happen. It also explains what to do. The map is ready.

words.meaning: people coming to see a place
the middle of the day
where two sides meet
curved things used for hanging
puts a sign on something

questions.q: When do students eat?
What has a star on the map?
Where are the hooks?

talk: How would you improve your first school-day explanation?
What useful detail would you add for a new student?
title: Our Class Guide

text: On the way to the library, Bea sees a baker opening his shop. A tray of bread is beside the door. “How do you help our town?” she asks. “I make food for people,” he replies. Bea writes one sentence in her notebook. She notices a bus driver across the street. The driver helps passengers reach different places. Bea cannot interview everyone today. She chooses the baker for her first helper card. It names his job and one useful action. Later, she hopes to explain his work with a real example. She leaves space under her sentence for a picture and a question.

words.meaning: a person who makes bread and cakes
a flat object for carrying things
people traveling in a vehicle
something a person does
ask someone questions about their life or work

questions.q: Where is Bea going?
Which helper does Bea choose?
What does the bus driver help passengers do?

talk: How does one worker help people in a town?
What would you ask that worker about their day?
title: People Who Help

text: Bea returns to the bakery with her helper card. Her first sentence said that the baker makes food. Now she has a clearer example. Yesterday, the baker prepared small rolls for a community lunch. He counted them and packed them in clean boxes. The lunch team collected the boxes before the shop became busy. “Your work helped people share a meal,” Bea says. “Thank you.” The baker asks what she will put on her card. Bea describes the job, the people it helps and the useful action. She adds a drawing of the boxes. Her card now explains more than a job name.

words.meaning: a place where bread is made or sold
made something ready
people living or working in the same area
came and took something away
put things into a container

questions.q: What did the baker prepare?
Who collected the boxes?
What does Bea draw?

talk: What example would show how your chosen helper helps?
How can you thank someone with a clear reason?
title: Thank a Helper

text: After school, Elin opens a group chat to check a rehearsal time. Ten minutes later, she is still looking at pictures. Her brother asks why she has not started her homework. “I came here for one message,” she says, “but every post led to another.” He suggests deleting the app. Elin does not want to lose the group where her friends arrange music practice. Instead, she draws a simple map of her online day. One part is useful: checking plans and sharing a recording. Another part is less useful: opening the feed whenever a task feels difficult. “What would you change first?” her brother asks. Elin chooses one small experiment. She will check the rehearsal chat after dinner, then leave her phone outside the room while she studies. She writes down her reason beside the plan. At the end of the course, she wants to explain whether that change helped and what she would keep.

words.meaning: practice before a performance
a changing list of online posts
plan how something will happen
a planned way to try an idea
sound or video saved to play again

questions.q: Why does Elin first open the chat?
Which activity does she want to keep?
Where will she leave her phone while studying?

talk: Which part of an online routine would you keep, and why?
How could you tell whether one small change was useful?
title: My Online Day

text: A youth club is discussing whether social platforms should limit teenagers' time. Noor supports a limit. “A feed does not have a natural stopping point,” she says. “A clear boundary could help people leave before a short visit becomes a long evening.” Felix disagrees with a single rule for everyone. He uses a group chat to organize a volunteer project. Some evenings, he needs more time to answer questions and share plans. Noor replies that essential messages could be treated differently from endless scrolling. Felix asks who would decide which activities count as essential. Their leader writes two concerns on the board: help people stop, and keep useful communication available. The group considers a warning that users can adjust, but that idea raises another question. Would people ignore it? Nobody has a complete answer yet. Before voting, the club asks each speaker to give one benefit, one possible problem and a reason the other side might find convincing.

words.meaning: a limit showing where something stops
needed for an important purpose
sharing information with other people
change something to suit a need
giving good reasons to believe something

questions.q: Who supports a time limit?
What does Felix organize online?
What adjustable option does the group consider?

talk: What should a fair platform rule protect?
How would you reply to the strongest reason on the other side?
title: Rules for Platforms

text: Elin returns to the map of her online day. Her original plan was to check the rehearsal chat after dinner and keep her phone outside the study room. She explains the result to her brother. “The quiet room helped me finish a difficult task,” she says. “But once I missed a last-minute change to rehearsal.” He asks whether she will abandon the plan. Elin thinks the problem needs a smaller repair. She will check the group once before starting work and once when she finishes. If a rehearsal is happening that evening, she will ask a friend to call about urgent changes. She keeps music messages but turns off alerts from the picture feed. Her new explanation has more than a rule. It names the useful part of social media, the interruption she wants to reduce and the cost of her choice. Elin does not claim that everyone should copy her routine. She can now give a reason for the change that suits her own day.

words.meaning: needing attention very soon
signals that tell you something has happened
something that breaks your attention or activity
stop following a plan
a usual order of activities

questions.q: What did Elin miss?
Who could call about urgent changes?
Which alerts does she turn off?

talk: How would you revise an online plan that partly worked?
What reason would make your proposed change convincing to someone else?
title: My Better Online Day

text: At a school careers table, Jamil picks up a card about bicycle repair. He enjoys finding out why small machines stop working, but he has never watched a mechanic for a whole day. His partner asks him to describe the job rather than just say it sounds interesting. Jamil imagines checking a brake, listening to a customer's problem and explaining what needs repair. He thinks patience and clear communication would matter as much as using tools. “Which part could you try safely now?” his partner asks. Jamil could learn the names of bicycle parts and observe a trained adult repairing a wheel. He would not test an unfamiliar repair on somebody's bike without help. He writes a short introduction to the role, then adds one reason it might suit him. There are still questions about training and the daily workload. For his course task, he keeps the card and leaves space to describe a next step when he knows more.

words.meaning: a person who repairs machines
a part that slows or stops a vehicle
staying calm when something takes time
watch carefully to learn
the amount of work someone has

questions.q: Which job interests Jamil?
Who could he observe repairing a wheel?
What does he keep for his course task?

talk: What job could you try, and which part interests you?
How could you explore that job safely before choosing it?
title: A Job I Could Try

text: A workshop wants to offer a short learning placement to teenagers. Two students discuss whether it should be paid. Mara argues that a student's time has value, especially when the student completes useful tasks. Payment could also make the placement possible for someone who must pay for travel. Dev agrees that access matters, but worries about a small workshop's budget. Teaching a beginner can take time away from normal work. If every placement costs more than the workshop can afford, it may offer none. Mara replies that a business should not use the word “learning” to hide ordinary unpaid work. Dev suggests separating observation from work that benefits the business. They both want clear hours, safe tasks and a named adult who can answer questions. Before deciding, they ask what the placement actually includes. Their debate is no longer only about money. It is also about whether the student receives real teaching and whether people with different resources can take part.

words.meaning: a short period of learning in a workplace
money given for work or something bought
the chance to enter or take part
a plan for money available and spent
careful watching to learn

questions.q: What workplace offers the placement?
What travel need does Mara mention?
What does Dev suggest separating from useful work?

talk: Which parts of a learning placement should be paid, and why?
What information would you need before deciding whether the offer is fair?
title: A Fair First Job

text: Jamil reads his first careers card again. He still wants to try bicycle repair, but his description now goes beyond “I like machines.” He explains that a mechanic must identify a fault, choose a safe repair and tell a customer what has changed. During a supervised visit, he watched an adult ask questions before touching a bike. The rider's description helped reveal a loose part. Jamil had expected the job to begin with tools; instead, it began with listening. For his next step, he plans to label the parts on a drawing and practice explaining a simple problem to a partner. He will ask the workshop which beginner course teaches safe basic checks. His partner wants to know why this role still suits him. “I enjoy careful problem solving,” Jamil says, “and I want to get better at explaining my thinking.” His final card includes the role, a reason and a realistic skill-building plan rather than a promise that he already knows the job.

words.meaning: something wrong that stops proper working
watched and guided by a responsible person
not firmly fixed in place
possible in the actual situation
find and name what something is

questions.q: What did the mechanic do before touching the bike?
What problem did the rider's description help reveal?
What will Jamil label?

talk: How has your job idea changed after learning about its tasks?
What realistic next step would help you build a useful skill?
title: My Next Step

text: Nell is choosing an activity for the school sports afternoon. Her friend wants to join a large football team, but Nell would rather try badminton. She likes games with short turns and a clear space to cover. “Does that mean you dislike working with people?” her friend asks. Nell explains that badminton can involve a partner too. What matters to her is having time to practice a movement before using it in a match. She has watched other students warm up, hit the shuttle and collect it when a rally ends. She has not yet learned how to control her shots. On her first sport card, she writes the activity, who can play and one reason it might suit her. The teacher reminds her that a first choice is not a permanent label. She can try another activity later. Nell keeps her card so she can give a more useful invitation to a newcomer at the course's end.

words.meaning: a game hitting a shuttle over a net
the object hit in badminton
a series of hits during a game
lasting without a planned ending
someone who has recently joined

questions.q: Which activity does Nell choose?
What has Nell not learned to control?
What does she keep?

talk: Why might one sport suit the way you like to learn?
What could trying a different activity teach you about yourself?
title: One Sport for Me

text: A school has enough space for one sports club after lessons. The current club plays only basketball. Hana argues for a wider choice. Some students want team matches, while others would prefer running, dance or individual practice. A choice could bring in people who do not enjoy the present club. Joel supports the idea but asks how it would work. The school has limited equipment and only two adults available to supervise. Offering every activity at once could leave groups without enough guidance. Hana proposes changing the activity each month instead. Joel worries that beginners would lose practice just as they started to improve. The group considers keeping one regular club and adding occasional trial sessions. That plan still needs a room, a timetable and somebody to lead it. Their debate shows that “more choice” can mean several different things. Before making a request, they decide to ask students which activities they would actually attend.

words.meaning: for one person rather than a group
watch and guide people doing an activity
help in deciding or learning something
a chance to try before deciding
go to and take part in

questions.q: Which sport does the current club play?
How many adults can supervise?
What does Hana propose changing each month?

talk: Which version of a wider sports choice would be practical?
How could a school listen to students without promising more than it can offer?
title: More Ways to Join

text: Nell is helping a new student choose a sports session. She brings the badminton card she wrote earlier, but now adds details from practice. “You hit a shuttle across a net,” she explains. “You can play with a partner, and you take turns serving.” The newcomer says he is nervous about making mistakes in front of others. Nell suggests a practice court where students work on short rallies before keeping score. She does not promise that badminton is easy or right for everyone. He will need suitable shoes, space around the court and help with the first movements. She explains why it suits her: she enjoys quick decisions and seeing a shot improve after repeated practice. Then she asks what he enjoys. He prefers moving with one partner to joining a big team. They agree to try one supervised session and talk afterward. Nell's invitation now gives useful information, a personal reason and an honest chance to decide.

words.meaning: starting a point by hitting the shuttle
worried about what might happen
a marked area for playing a sport
right for a particular purpose
done again and again

questions.q: What does Nell suggest before keeping score?
What does the newcomer prefer to a big team?
What do they agree to try?

talk: How would you invite a newcomer without putting pressure on them?
Which practical details would make your sport recommendation more useful?
title: My Sport Invitation

text: When Dara needs a quiet break, she chooses a short piece of instrumental music. It begins with a soft drum pattern, then a low melody enters. There are no words to follow. Her friend asks why she chooses it instead of a louder song. Dara taps the rhythm on the table. “The beat is steady, but little sounds change around it,” she says. “It reminds me of watching rain from indoors.” Her friend notices the melody but finds the repeated beat dull. Dara is surprised that they hear the same piece differently. She writes a first introduction for her course task: what the music sounds like, when she listens and why it matters to her. She does not need to persuade her friend to enjoy it. She wants to describe her choice clearly enough for another person to imagine the sound. Later, she hopes to notice more than whether a piece feels calm or energetic.

words.meaning: played with instruments rather than sung words
a sequence of musical notes
a repeated pattern of beats
continuing at a regular pace
full of energy

questions.q: What begins the piece?
What does the music remind Dara of?
What does her friend find dull?

talk: What sounds would help you describe a piece you enjoy?
Why might two people respond differently to the same music?
title: The Music I Choose

text: Dara prepares a new introduction to the instrumental piece from her first lesson. She listens for changes instead of calling the whole piece “quiet.” The drum enters alone. A low melody follows, and a higher sound answers it. Near the middle, the drum stops briefly, leaving more space around the notes. Dara plays that section for her friend. “That pause makes the next beat feel stronger,” she says. She also explains her personal reason for choosing the piece. Listening to a familiar pattern gives her a small break between busy tasks, while the changing sounds keep it interesting. Her friend still prefers music with words, but now understands her choice. Dara's final introduction names the instruments she can hear, describes one contrast and connects it to her own experience. She avoids claiming that the music will make everyone feel the same way. A good introduction can help a listener notice something without telling them what to like.

words.meaning: one part of a larger piece
for a short time
a clear difference between two things
already known to you
an arrangement that repeats

questions.q: What stops near the middle?
What music does Dara's friend prefer?
What does Dara describe in her final introduction?

talk: Which small change in a piece would you point out to a listener?
How could you explain why music matters without making a claim for everyone?
title: My Music Introduction

text: Milo has watched a short comedy called “One Bike, Two Plans.” It follows two friends who want to organize a neighborhood ride but have different ideas about the route. One loves careful maps; the other wants to make decisions as they go. Their disagreements create small surprises rather than cruel jokes. Milo wants to recommend the film without giving away its ending. His partner asks him for three things: the kind of story, its starting situation and one reason to watch. Milo explains that it is a comedy about friendship and planning. He likes how the camera shows both friends' reactions before either speaks. His partner usually chooses mysteries, so Milo mentions the question that keeps him watching: will they find a plan they can both accept? He stops before answering it. For his course task, he writes this first recommendation. Later, he will try to replace general praise with clearer details from the film.

words.meaning: the path taken to reach a place
responses to something that happens
suggest something someone may enjoy
the final part of a story
words showing approval

questions.q: What kind of film did Milo watch?
What do the friends want to organize?
What does Milo avoid giving away?

talk: What detail would make you curious without spoiling a story?
How would you describe a screen story to someone with different tastes?
title: What I Watch

text: Milo rewrites his recommendation for “One Bike, Two Plans.” His first version explained the starting problem but called the acting simply “good.” Now he chooses a moment that supports his opinion. At a crossroads, one friend unfolds a large map while the other studies the clouds. The scene lets their different planning styles appear through actions, not a long explanation. Milo describes the camera staying on both faces when they disagree. It makes the silence part of the joke. He still leaves the final route secret. His review also includes a fair limit: viewers who want fast action may find the slower conversations less exciting. His partner says that detail helps her decide whether to watch. Milo's final reason is specific. The film shows friends listening without becoming identical, and its gentle humor comes from ordinary choices. He can now give a clear, spoiler-free recommendation rather than promising that every viewer will enjoy the same things.

words.meaning: a place where roads meet
opens something that was folded
a time with no sound
people watching a film or programme
clear and about one particular thing

questions.q: Where does one friend unfold a map?
What does the other friend study?
What does Milo keep secret?

talk: What example would support your review without revealing the ending?
How could a fair limitation make a recommendation more helpful?
title: My Short Review

text:
At the edge of the school courtyard, Sora notices a chalk circle around an empty patch of ground. A folded blue cloth lies on a bench nearby, and a single wet shoeprint leads away from the circle. The rest of the paving looks dry. Her friend Anton immediately suggests a treasure hunt. Perhaps the circle marks a place where someone has hidden a clue. Sora enjoys the idea, but asks what each detail actually supports. A circle could mark the size of an object. The cloth might belong to somebody who was cleaning. A wet print shows that a shoe was wet; it does not explain why.

They make three columns in a notebook: observation, possible explanation and question. Sora describes the circle without calling it a secret sign. Anton notes the cloth's colour without deciding who owned it. Together, they record the print's position and leave its cause open. Their first mystery account uses all three clues, but neither student thinks it is a solution yet. Before looking for more information, they explain the scene to a partner who has not seen it. If the partner can picture the courtyard without sharing their guesses, they have described it fairly. Later, they will return to their account and test whether an explanation can connect the clues without inventing missing events.

words.meaning: a hard surface made for walking
something you notice directly
gives a reason to accept an idea
the place where something is
a description of what happened

questions.q: What surrounds the empty patch?
Where is the blue cloth?
What does the print show for certain?

talk: Which explanation fits the clues without adding too many assumptions?
What question would you ask before treating your explanation as a solution?
title: A Puzzling Scene

text:
Sora and Anton return to their courtyard notes after speaking with the art teacher. The class had been planning a large drawing on the paving. The chalk circle marked space for its central pattern. The teacher had left a blue cloth on the bench while washing chalk from a student's hands. That student then crossed the courtyard with wet shoes. This account connects the circle, the cloth and the print without requiring a hidden treasure.

Sora prepares her final explanation, but Anton asks whether the teacher's account is enough. A garden group could also have marked a circle for a plant pot, used a cloth during cleaning and left wet footprints after watering. Sora agrees that the original clues alone would not distinguish those stories. The teacher's description adds information from someone who was there, while a sketch of the planned drawing provides another check.

Their final talk separates those layers. First, they state the three original observations. Next, they explain how the art activity could have produced each one. Finally, they acknowledge the gardening alternative and say what makes the art explanation stronger. Sora removes the phrase “obviously a treasure hunt” from their first notes. A fair solution does not need to sound certain at every step. It needs a clear connection between evidence and explanation, plus an honest account of what remains untested.

words.meaning: in the middle
needing something to be true or present
tell the difference between things
recognize and mention something
not yet checked

questions.q: What did the circle mark?
What alternative do they consider?
What provides another check on the teacher's account?
questions.a: a sketch of the planned drawing

talk: How would you explain three clues while keeping observations separate from guesses?
What would make an alternative explanation strong enough to investigate?
title: My Fair Solution

text: Talia has saved enough for either a drawing kit or a ticket to a weekend art workshop. The two choices cost about the same, but they offer different things. The kit would stay with her and let her practice whenever she has time. The workshop would give her a chance to ask an artist questions and try materials she has not used before. Her friend asks which choice is better. Talia says she needs to compare them with her own goal, not only their price. She wants to learn how to draw moving people. She already has ordinary pencils, but no one to give feedback on her sketches. A workshop may help with that, although it also needs a journey and a free afternoon. Talia writes a first spending choice with its trade-off: teaching for one day instead of new tools she could keep. She leaves the decision open until she checks the full cost and what the workshop actually includes.

words.meaning: a set of tools for an activity
comments that help someone improve
what you give up to gain something
has as one of its parts
something you are trying to achieve

questions.q: What two choices is Talia comparing?
questions.a: a drawing kit or a ticket

questions.q: What does Talia want to learn to draw?
What does she already have?

talk: What information matters besides price when choosing what to buy?
How would you explain the trade-off in one spending choice?
title: A Choice to Make

text: Talia checks the art workshop before making her final spending plan. The ticket includes materials, but not transport. The session also focuses on painting landscapes rather than drawing people. She returns to her first note and changes her decision. Instead of buying the full kit or that ticket, she will keep using her pencils and save for a more suitable workshop. Her friend asks whether keeping the money means she has done nothing. Talia disagrees. She has learned to check the full cost, compare the offer with her goal and leave room for a journey in her budget. She sets a limit: any future ticket and transport together must fit within her savings. For now, she joins a free drawing group where members exchange sketches and comments. Her final explanation names what she wanted, what she found out and what she is giving up. She postpones new materials, but gains more time to practice and a clearer rule for her next purchase.

words.meaning: travel from one place to another
pictures of outdoor places
right for someone's needs
moves something to a later time
something you buy

questions.q: What is not included in the workshop ticket?
What does the session focus on?
What group does Talia join?

talk: How could new information change your first spending choice?
What limit would help you balance your goal with the full cost?
title: My Spending Plan

text: A narrow path links Ivo's school with a small park. On windy mornings, light food wrappers collect against the fence. Ivo wants to suggest one local action for his course task. His first idea is to organize a clean-up every Friday. That would make the path clearer, but his partner asks where the wrappers come from. Ivo has not checked. He assumes people drop them, although an overflowing bin might also be involved. They walk past the area with a teacher and describe what they can see without touching the waste. Most wrappers lie near a bin whose lid does not close. Farther along the path, there are fewer. Ivo writes down the issue, his proposed action and its possible effect. He also notes a question: would cleaning the path solve the cause or only remove the result? His opening plan is useful but incomplete. He will keep looking for a small change that people can maintain, not simply a large promise about saving the planet.

words.meaning: covers around food or other items
a barrier around a place
too full to keep its contents inside
suggested for people to consider
keep working well over time

questions.q: What collects against the fence?
What is Ivo's first idea?
What problem does the bin have?

talk: How could you find the cause of a local environmental problem?
What effect would you expect from one small action near you?
title: One Change Near Us

text: Ivo brings his path notes to the school council. His first idea was a weekly clean-up, but he now proposes asking the park caretaker to repair the bin lid. A closed lid could keep light wrappers from blowing out before collection. He explains the benefit carefully: it would reduce one source of litter, not stop every piece of rubbish along the path. There is a cost too. Somebody must arrange the repair and check that the lid still closes after use. His partner suggests making a polite request with a drawing of the problem. They will also ask adults how the remaining waste can be handled safely. Ivo compares the new plan with his original one. Cleaning still has a place, but preventing rubbish from escaping may reduce repeated work. His final talk names one action, its expected effect and a possible difficulty. The council can now respond to a practical request instead of a general wish for a cleaner park.

words.meaning: a person who looks after a place
make something smaller or less
where something comes from
stopping something before it happens
something you politely ask someone to do

questions.q: Who might repair the lid?
What could a closed lid keep from blowing out?
What will the students include with their request?

talk: How does your final local action address the cause of the problem?
What difficulty should you explain honestly when asking people to support it?
title: A Local Plan

text: The debate club begins with a school-rule question: should homework have a fixed time limit? Reva makes a clear claim. She thinks a limit would help students plan the rest of their evening. Instead of calling all homework useless, she describes a concrete problem from the club's practice story. A student finished one short task, then spent a long time guessing what a second task required. Reva argues that clear instructions and a reasonable limit could both help. Ben replies that some students need more practice than others. A single limit might reduce the time available to someone who wants extra help. Reva accepts that objection and suggests optional practice beyond the required task. The group labels three parts of her answer: claim, evidence and reply. Her example does not prove that one rule will work everywhere. It makes her reasoning visible. She keeps those labels on a card so she can use them again for a different school rule at the end of the course.

words.meaning: an idea you ask others to accept
information used to support an idea
a reason for disagreeing
something you may choose but need not do
the steps connecting information to a conclusion

questions.q: What fixed limit does the club discuss?
What does Ben think some students need?
What does Reva suggest beyond the required task?

talk: What evidence would help you judge a homework rule?
How could you accept part of an objection without abandoning your claim?
title: One Clear Claim

text: A class considers allowing AI tools to help plan homework. Ellis supports using a tool to list possible steps before writing. In the class's example, a large project becomes easier to start when it is divided into smaller tasks. Ellis still wants the student to choose the steps and do the actual thinking. Priya worries that a polished plan can hide mistakes. A tool might suggest checking a source that does not exist or omit a part of the assignment. She would rather students ask a teacher when instructions are unclear. Ellis replies that checking the plan could itself be a learning task, but agrees that the teacher should see how the tool was used. They propose testing one sample plan together before choosing a rule. The debate turns on a distinction: receiving a suggestion is not the same as knowing it is reliable. Each side must explain where responsibility stays with the learner, and what support would make the proposed use fair.

words.meaning: leave something out
a piece of work someone must complete
able to be trusted for a purpose
a duty to make or check a decision
an idea offered for someone to consider

questions.q: What does Ellis want the tool to list?
Who does Priya prefer students to ask?
What do the classmates propose testing?

talk: Which parts of planning should stay with the student?
What check would make a proposed AI rule more convincing?
title: Two Sides of AI

text: Two groups argue about screens in lessons. One wants fewer screens because notifications and open tabs can pull attention away from a task. The other wants teachers to keep digital tools when they reveal something a printed page cannot. Their teacher gives them a fictional lesson record to examine. During a science activity, students used a close-up image to compare leaf edges. Later, several students opened unrelated messages while writing their observations. The same device supported one activity and interrupted another. Jo argues for deciding by purpose rather than counting every minute as equally useful. Amir replies that a purpose-based rule may be harder to supervise than a simple screen-free period. Jo suggests closing unnecessary tabs and putting devices away after the image task. The group notices that their evidence supports a narrow conclusion about this lesson, not a claim that screens always help or always harm. They revise their arguments to include that limit before preparing a reply to the other side.

words.meaning: signals about new messages or events
not connected to the subject
things noticed and recorded
watch and guide an activity
an idea reached after considering information

questions.q: What did students compare in the science activity?
What interrupted the later task?
What does Jo suggest closing?

talk: How could a rule distinguish useful screen tasks from distractions?
What limit should you mention when using evidence from one lesson?
title: Evidence on Screens

text: At a practice debate, Wen argues that teenagers doing useful work during an internship should be paid. A partner objects that a small repair shop may spend more time teaching a beginner than receiving help. Wen first wants to answer, “That is unfair.” Then she realizes the reply does not address the concern. She asks what the student would actually do. Watching a skilled worker for an hour is different from completing tasks for several weeks. The partner agrees, but says supervision still has a cost. Wen suggests that a placement could describe teaching time and work time separately, with clear arrangements for each. She also asks whether travel costs would stop some students taking part. Her revised reply recognizes the shop's difficulty while keeping the question of access visible. The club cannot settle every payment detail from this example. It can practice a fair reply: state the objection accurately, answer it with a reason and explain which part of the original claim still stands.

words.meaning: a period of learning through workplace experience
something someone is worried about
watching and guiding someone's work
plans agreed for how something will happen
without changing or misrepresenting the information

questions.q: Which workplace does the partner mention?
What cost may stop some students taking part?
What should a fair reply state accurately?

talk: How would you restate an opponent's concern fairly?
What information could change your view of a particular internship?
title: A Fair Reply

text: Reva takes out the claim, evidence and reply card from her first debate. This time, the school rule concerns using students' home languages when possible. She claims that learners should be able to explain a difficult idea in a familiar language before practicing the class language. Her evidence comes from a practice scenario: a student explains a science process to a partner, then tries the same explanation with newly learned terms. The first explanation reveals understanding that a short answer had hidden. Ben replies that a teacher may not know every language in the room and needs a way to check the work. Reva accepts the practical problem. She suggests a final explanation the teacher can follow, with a diagram or glossary if needed. Her closing statement includes a benefit, an example and a limit instead of pretending the rule has no costs. Compared with her first debate, she now makes the other side's strongest concern part of her answer. The card's three labels remain the same; the reasoning beneath them has grown.

words.meaning: already known and understood
words with particular meanings in a subject
a list explaining special words
an imagined situation used for discussion
possible to do in the actual situation

questions.q: Which languages does the new rule concern?
What subject appears in the practice scenario?
What could help the teacher follow an explanation?

talk: How would you connect a claim, evidence and reply about a school rule?
Which part of your reasoning has improved since your first debate?
title: Make the Case Again

text: Finn tells a partner about a small surprise on his walk home. First, he heard a soft ringing sound near a tree. He stopped and looked around. A bicycle stood beside the path, but nobody was riding it. Then he noticed a little bell hanging from a branch. The wind moved it against the leaves. Finn took a picture instead of touching it. Later, he showed the picture to his neighbor. She had hung the bell beside a bird feeder. Finn's story has a beginning, a discovery and an ending. His partner can follow the order without guessing what happened first.

words.meaning: making a clear bell sound
a part growing out from a tree
something you find out or notice
a container holding food for birds
the way things come one after another

questions.q: Where does Finn hear the sound?
What is hanging from a branch?
Who had hung the bell?

talk: What small moment could you tell as a story with three steps?
Which details help a listener picture the discovery?
title: Describe a Moment

text: Two partners are planning a class display. Lena wants a large drawing. Finn wants a model made from boxes. Lena speaks first, then asks Finn to explain his idea. “A model would let people look from different sides,” he says. She agrees, but points out that their table is small. Finn listens and changes his plan. They could make a small model with a drawing behind it. Lena offers to draw the background while Finn measures the boxes. Both partners now have a job. They did not need to win an argument. They needed to understand the other idea and build a shared plan.

a small copy or planned version
the part shown behind the main thing
finds the size of something
belonging to or done by several people

questions.q: What does Lena want to make?
What limits the model's size?
Who will draw the background?

talk: How could you invite a quieter partner to explain an idea?

title: Speak with a Partner

text: Finn listens to the short introduction he made at the start. He said his name and that he liked making things. Now he adds a choice and two reasons. “I would join a model club,” he says. “I enjoy finding ways to build strong shapes. I also want to learn from people with different ideas.” His partner asks for an example. Finn describes the small display he planned with Lena. Their different suggestions became one shared design. He pauses between his reasons instead of rushing. His stronger answer is still simple. The listener now knows his interests and reasons for joining.

words.meaning: the first words explaining who or what
one thing selected from different possibilities
the forms of objects
a plan for how something will look
stops briefly before continuing

questions.q: What club would Finn join?

What does he do between reasons?

title: My Stronger Answer
